domain_label: Explainability & Onboarding — Progressive Disclosure & Help Systems
purpose: A method for making a zero-tooltip study app self-explaining through layered information reveal — the tiny-caption -> hover-card -> 'more' panel -> guide-page disclosure ladder, first-run/empty-state onboarding, and a single-sourced help system whose deepest rungs state the app's honesty tags honestly (e.g. a Weakness 'confidence 80%' is a fixed heuristic constant, not a probability), kept honest by tagging every load-bearing claim and refusing to invent HCI citations or app behaviors.
assumptions: no observed dataset or usability study is supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and every design-pattern recommendation is an ESTIMATE synthesized from HCI practice, not a measured result on this app

the app today has ZERO tooltips, no title= hover hints, no onboarding, and no guide layer, so this KB designs a greenfield help layer rather than refining an existing one [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9]

HCI pattern names and standards (progressive disclosure, WCAG content-on-hover requirements, onboarding-tour patterns) are carried from general domain knowledge and tagged ESTIMATE — to source-verify because no HCI source was fetched and verified in this grounding session

the deep 'why' derivations of algorithmic decisions (why this card, why this weakness cause, why the plan shrank) are owned by the neighboring explainable-AI KB of this same specialist; this KB owns the DISCLOSURE MECHANICS that surface them and the honesty of what the deep rung says, not the reasoning itself
exclusions: the explainable-AI explanation-interface content for scheduler/diagnoser decisions (neighboring uxguide KB) beyond requiring the ladder's deep rung to present it honestly and link to it
the plain-language / technical-communication rewriting rules for a single explanation string (neighboring uxguide KB) beyond naming microcopy as rung 1 of the ladder
the actual React/shadcn implementation, the graph-view rendering, and the color system (owned by viz and by the app's own components) beyond specifying where a disclosure affordance attaches
the correctness of the underlying BKT/Elo/FSRS math and the E1-E4 diagnosis rules (owned by learner + sysloops); this KB only governs how those outputs are explained to the user

competency_questions.question: What is progressive disclosure and why is it the right frame for making a zero-tooltip study app self-explaining?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states the show-the-minimum / defer-detail-on-demand principle, names the app's zero-tooltip starting point as FACT from APP_RECON §5.9, and ties disclosure to reducing initial cognitive load without hiding capability

competency_questions.question: What are the ordered rungs of the disclosure ladder and how does a user climb from one to the next?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names the four rungs tiny caption -> hover card -> 'more'/expandable panel -> guide page as an on-demand escalation each triggered by an explicit user action, not auto-expansion

competency_questions.question: What belongs on rung 1, the inline microcopy caption, and what must NOT be pushed off it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes the always-visible inline label/caption as the cheapest rung, and states that information required to use the control must stay on rung 1 rather than be hidden in a tooltip

competency_questions.question: How does rung 2, the tooltip/hover card, work, and how is it made accessible rather than hover-only?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: specifies hover/focus/tap triggers, an info-icon affordance, show/hide timing, and the dismissible-hoverable-persistent accessibility requirement for content shown on hover or focus

competency_questions.question: What is rung 3, the 'more' / expandable panel, and when does a concept need it above a tooltip?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes an in-context expandable popover/panel opened by a 'more' or '?' action that holds a paragraph-plus explanation too large for a tooltip but still contextual, keeping the user on the page

competency_questions.question: What is rung 4, the guide page, and what role does it play as the deepest and most durable rung?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes a dedicated, linkable, searchable guide page as the canonical single source for each concept that shallower rungs quote and deep-link into

competency_questions.question: What are the tooltip and disclosure anti-patterns this help layer must avoid?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names tooltip-hell, essential-info-in-a-tooltip, hover-only-on-touch, and hijacking the pointer, and gives the avoidance rule for each

competency_questions.question: How should first-run onboarding introduce the app, and how are onboarding anti-patterns like the tour dump and the onboarding cliff avoided?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: distinguishes empty-state/contextual onboarding from upfront product tours, ties onboarding to the same disclosure ladder, and names the forced-tour-dump and onboarding-cliff failures with mitigations

competency_questions.question: How is the help system architected so tooltips, panels and the guide page stay single-sourced and contextually triggered rather than drifting apart?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes one canonical content source per concept, contextual '?' triggers placed next to the confusing element, and a maintenance rule that shallow rungs are derived from the guide-page source

competency_questions.question: How must the deep rungs present the app's honesty tags, e.g. the Weakness 'confidence 80%'?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states that the explanation must say confidence % is a fixed per-rule heuristic constant (0.4-0.8) not a computed probability [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4a], and generalizes to labeling every surfaced heuristic honestly

competency_questions.question: Which app surfaces get which rungs, and how deep should each concept's ladder go?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: maps concrete surfaces (StatsRow 'New 24', Weakness 'confidence 80%', DayBox fill, mastery bars, FK/CC labels) to rungs and states an escalation-depth budget so not every element gets four rungs

competency_questions.question: What is the recommended progressive-disclosure help-layer verdict, including information scent and not re-nagging dismissed tips?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: commits to a 4-rung accessible ladder + empty-state onboarding + single-sourced honest guide, with visible information scent and dismissed-tip persistence, and an explicit no-go on forced tours and hover-only tooltips

glossary.definition: The HCI design principle of showing only the minimum information and controls needed for the common case and deferring advanced or explanatory detail to secondary surfaces the user opens on demand, reducing initial cognitive load without removing capability [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; widely attributed to Nielsen-tradition usability practice].

This KB's ordered escalation of help surfaces for one concept: rung 1 inline microcopy caption, rung 2 tooltip/hover card, rung 3 'more'/expandable in-context panel, rung 4 dedicated guide page; each rung is entered by an explicit user action and holds progressively more detail.

The visible cue (typically a small info 'i' or '?' icon, an underline, or an affordance) that signals a deeper explanation exists and is reachable, letting a user decide whether to climb the disclosure ladder [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; information-foraging term].

Rung 2: a small transient overlay revealing a short explanation when the user hovers, focuses, or taps an affordance; must be dismissible, hoverable, and persistent to be accessible, and must never be the only place essential information lives.

Rung 4: a dedicated, linkable, searchable in-app help page that is the canonical single source of truth for what each number, control and screen means; shallower rungs quote it and deep-link into its anchors.

The help shown to a brand-new user with no data — empty-state prompts, one contextual tip at the moment of need, and a path into the guide page — as opposed to a modal product tour shown before the user has any context.

The failure where onboarding help appears once and never again, so a user who dismisses or forgets it has no way back to the explanation; avoided by persistent information scent and an always-reachable guide page [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The rule that when a disclosure rung explains an app number, it must state that number's true nature — e.g. the Weakness 'confidence 80%' is a fixed heuristic constant per diagnosis rule (0.4-0.8), not a computed posterior probability [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4a] — rather than implying a rigor the value does not have.

The content-architecture discipline of authoring each concept's explanation once (in the guide-page source) and generating the tooltip and panel copy from that source, so the rungs cannot drift into contradicting each other as the app changes.

The policy that not every UI element deserves all four rungs: trivial controls get rung 1 only, ambiguous numbers get rungs 1-2, algorithmic outputs (confidence, mastery, feasibility) earn rungs 3-4, so the help layer stays proportionate and maintainable.

nodes.definition: Frame the problem this KB solves: the study app is powerful but opaque — it shows figures like 'New 24', a Weakness 'confidence 80%', a DayBox filling in 5% increments, and FK/CC mastery bars with no explanation anywhere, because the app has ZERO tooltips, no title= hover hints, and no onboarding or guide layer [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9]. The job is to make the app self-explaining via layered on-demand help rather than a wall of upfront text, so a user can understand any surface without reading code. This KB owns the DISCLOSURE MECHANICS (the ladder, onboarding, help architecture, and the honesty of the deepest rung); the deep 'why' reasoning of algorithmic decisions is a neighboring KB [ESTIMATE — scope split is a design decision].

included: the zero-help starting state as the problem

pros.claim: Naming the zero-help starting state fixes the scope as greenfield help design rather than refinement
pros.example: treating 'New 24' and 'confidence 80%' as unexplained surfaces to be laddered, not existing tooltips to tweak

cons.claim: The mechanics-vs-reasoning split is a design judgment that can leave a seam between this KB and the explainable-AI KB
cons.example: a tooltip that needs the 'why this weakness' reasoning owned by the neighbor to be genuinely useful

failure_modes: treating help as an afterthought bolted on rather than a designed layer
claiming the app already has tooltips when it does not
acceptance_tests: the frame states the zero-tooltip starting point with the APP_RECON §5.9 citation, the self-explaining goal, and the mechanics-vs-reasoning scope split
revisit_triggers: the app adds a help layer that changes the starting state
the scope split with the explainable-AI KB is renegotiated
new opaque surfaces appear

base.update_signal: a change to the app's help starting state or the KB scope split revises the frame

nodes.definition: State the core principle: show the minimum needed for the common case and defer advanced or explanatory detail to secondary surfaces the user opens on demand, so the default view stays low-load while full capability and full explanation remain one deliberate step away [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; standard usability principle attributed to the Nielsen tradition]. Progressive disclosure trades a small cost (the user must act to see more) for a large benefit (novices are not overwhelmed and experts are not slowed). It is the organizing idea behind every rung of this KB's ladder: each successive surface reveals more only when asked, and nothing essential to using a control is hidden behind a reveal.

pros.claim: Deferring detail on demand keeps a dense study dashboard readable for a novice without stripping capability from an expert
pros.example: a clean Dashboard where every number is quietly explainable rather than annotated in place

cons.claim: Over-applied, disclosure buries information the user actually needs behind an extra click and hurts discoverability
cons.example: hiding what 'New 24' means so deeply that a new user never finds the explanation

failure_modes: hiding information required to operate a control
using disclosure as an excuse for a cluttered default that still overwhelms
acceptance_tests: the principle states show-minimum/defer-detail, gives the load-reduction rationale, and names the do-not-hide-essentials caveat, tagged ESTIMATE — to source-verify
revisit_triggers: users cannot find deferred explanations
the default view is judged too dense despite disclosure
a source verification updates the attribution

base.update_signal: a discoverability failure or a source verification revises the principle

nodes.definition: Define the visible cue that a deeper explanation exists and is reachable — typically a small info 'i' or '?' icon, a dotted underline, or a subtle affordance next to an ambiguous number or control [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; information-foraging concept]. Without scent, progressive disclosure fails silently: the detail exists but no user knows to look for it, reproducing the app's current opacity behind a nicer facade. Scent is the owner's 'small icon' that escalates to a deeper explanation; it must be present wherever a surface is not self-evident, discoverable by sight, and consistent so users learn that the icon always means 'more is here'.

included: the info/'?' icon as the reveal cue
why absent scent silently breaks disclosure
excluded: the content revealed after the cue

pros.claim: A consistent info-icon teaches users one gesture that always reveals more, making the whole ladder discoverable
pros.example: every explainable number carrying the same small 'i' so users learn to look for it

cons.claim: Scent icons add visual noise, and too many turn a clean view back into a cluttered one
cons.example: an 'i' beside every label so the dashboard looks annotated and busy

failure_modes: deferring detail with no visible cue that it exists
using inconsistent icons so users do not learn the gesture
acceptance_tests: scent is defined as the visible reveal cue, absent-scent is identified as a silent disclosure failure, and consistency of the affordance is required
revisit_triggers: users miss available explanations
scent icons are judged too noisy
a new affordance style is adopted

base.update_signal: a discoverability miss or a scent-noise complaint changes the affordance

nodes.definition: Define the ladder this KB is built around: four ordered rungs of increasing detail for one concept — rung 1 inline microcopy caption (always visible), rung 2 tooltip/hover card (short, on hover/focus/tap), rung 3 'more'/expandable in-context panel (a paragraph-plus, still on the page), rung 4 dedicated guide page (canonical, linkable). Each step is entered by an explicit user action, never auto-expansion, and each higher rung is a superset of the meaning below it. This is the owner's tiny-caption -> hover-card -> 'more' -> guide-page escalation made concrete [ESTIMATE — synthesis of standard help-surface tiers; to source-verify]. The ladder gives every explainable surface a predictable path from a one-word hint to a full page.

included: the four ordered rungs and their triggers
excluded: each rung's detailed mechanics (their own nodes)
which surface gets how many rungs

pros.claim: A fixed four-rung model gives every surface the same predictable escalation, so users learn one pattern for the whole app
pros.example: hovering any number for a hint and clicking 'more' for a panel, everywhere

cons.claim: A rigid ladder can be overkill for trivial controls and still too shallow for a genuinely complex screen
cons.example: forcing a four-rung ladder onto a self-evident 'Save' button

failure_modes: auto-expanding rungs instead of on-demand
skipping a rung so the jump from hint to guide page is too abrupt
acceptance_tests: the four rungs are named in order with their triggers, the explicit-action-per-step rule is stated, and higher rungs are shown to superset lower ones
revisit_triggers: a rung proves redundant or missing in practice
the escalation feels abrupt
a fifth surface type is proposed

base.update_signal: a redundant/missing rung or a new surface type changes the ladder

nodes.definition: Specify rung 1, the always-visible inline caption or label — the cheapest disclosure, requiring no user action. It renames or annotates a bare figure so its meaning is closer to self-evident: 'New 24' becomes 'New cards today: 24', a bare percentage gets a unit and subject. The governing rule is that information REQUIRED to operate or safely read a control stays on rung 1 and is never demoted into a tooltip, because a hidden essential is an accessibility and usability failure [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. Rung 1 handles the majority of ambiguity for free; higher rungs exist only for meaning that genuinely cannot fit inline without clutter.

included: handling most ambiguity without a reveal

pros.claim: Fixing a label inline resolves ambiguity with zero interaction and zero accessibility cost
pros.example: relabeling 'New 24' to 'New cards today: 24' so no hover is needed at all

cons.claim: Inline text competes for scarce space, so over-labeling re-clutters the exact dense view disclosure was meant to declutter
cons.example: every stat carrying a full sentence caption until the StatsRow overflows

failure_modes: demoting essential operating information into a tooltip
over-labeling until the layout is cluttered again
acceptance_tests: rung 1 is defined as the always-visible caption, the essentials-stay-inline rule is stated, and it is shown to resolve most ambiguity without a reveal
revisit_triggers: essential information is found only in a tooltip
inline captions overflow the layout
a relabel changes an established term

base.update_signal: a hidden-essential finding or layout overflow changes the rung-1 policy

nodes.definition: Specify rung 2, the tooltip/hover card: a small transient overlay revealing a short explanation (roughly one to three sentences) when the user hovers, keyboard-focuses, or taps an affordance carrying information scent. It is the first on-demand rung and the workhorse for 'what is this number' questions. Timing matters — a short show-delay avoids flicker on pass-through, and it must not vanish the instant the pointer leaves [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. Content is short by construction: anything needing a paragraph or interaction belongs on rung 3, and anything essential belongs on rung 1. The tooltip explains, it never holds the only copy of something the user must act on.

included: the length ceiling that pushes longer content up a rung

pros.claim: A short hover card answers 'what is this' in place at the moment of curiosity without navigation
pros.example: hovering the DayBox to read 'fills 5% per unit studied; check-mark at 100% of today's plan'

cons.claim: Tooltips are transient and easy to over-use, so packing meaning into them risks losing it and cluttering the interaction
cons.example: a tooltip crammed with a paragraph the user cannot read before it disappears

failure_modes: putting paragraph-length or interactive content in a transient tooltip
show/hide timing that flickers or vanishes too fast to read
acceptance_tests: rung 2 is defined as a short transient overlay on hover/focus/tap with sensible timing, and the length ceiling that escalates longer content to rung 3 is stated
revisit_triggers: tooltips are found holding paragraph content
users report flicker or premature dismissal
the affordance trigger set changes

base.update_signal: over-stuffed tooltips or timing complaints change the rung-2 spec

nodes.definition: Specify rung 3, the 'more' / expandable panel: an in-context popover, disclosure widget, or side panel opened by a 'more' link or '?' button that holds a paragraph-plus explanation, a small example, or a short list too large for a transient tooltip but not worth a full navigation away. It keeps the user on the current screen with the element still in view, which is exactly why it is the right home for a real explanation of an algorithmic output — how a mastery bar is aggregated, what the four E1-E4 weakness causes mean — while the guide page holds the exhaustive version. Rung 3 is persistent until dismissed, so unlike a tooltip it can carry content the user needs time to read [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

included: the in-context expandable panel opened by 'more'/'?'
hosting real algorithmic-output explanations while staying on-page

pros.claim: A persistent in-context panel lets a user read a real explanation without losing their place on the page
pros.example: clicking 'more' on a Weakness to read what 'missing_prereq' means with the element still visible

cons.claim: Panels occupy layout and, if overloaded, become mini-pages that would have been better as the guide page
cons.example: an expandable panel that grows into three scrolling screens of text

failure_modes: making the panel transient so it dismisses before reading
overloading it until it should have been the guide page
acceptance_tests: rung 3 is defined as a persistent in-context 'more'/'?' panel that hosts paragraph-plus explanations on-page and escalates exhaustive content to rung 4
revisit_triggers: panels grow into de-facto pages
a panel dismisses before users finish reading
on-page space becomes constrained

base.update_signal: panels overgrowing or dismissing early change the rung-3 spec

nodes.definition: Specify rung 4, the guide page: a dedicated, linkable, searchable in-app page that is the canonical single source of truth for what every number, control and screen means, organized so each concept has a stable anchor the shallower rungs deep-link into. It is the deepest and most durable rung — the place a user lands from a tooltip's 'learn more', and the reference that survives when a one-time onboarding tip is long gone, directly countering the onboarding cliff. Because the app has no guide layer at all today [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9], this is greenfield: the guide page is authored once per concept and every shallower surface is derived from or points at it, which is what keeps the ladder consistent.

included: the dedicated linkable searchable guide page as canonical source
per-concept stable anchors for deep links
its role against the onboarding cliff

pros.claim: A canonical guide page gives every explanation one durable home that outlives transient tips and anchors the whole ladder
pros.example: a tooltip's 'learn more' deep-linking to the guide-page anchor for 'confidence'

cons.claim: A guide page is only as good as its upkeep; if it is not maintained it drifts from the app and misleads
cons.example: a guide page still describing an old label after the UI was renamed

failure_modes: letting the guide page drift from the current app
making it a dead wall of text with no deep-link anchors
acceptance_tests: rung 4 is defined as a dedicated linkable searchable canonical guide page with per-concept anchors, its greenfield status is cited to APP_RECON §5.9, and its role against the onboarding cliff is stated
revisit_triggers: the guide page drifts from the UI
deep links break
search over the guide fails users

base.update_signal: guide-page drift or broken deep links change the rung-4 design

nodes.definition: Constrain rung 2 so it is not hover-only, which would exclude keyboard and touch users and screen readers. Content shown on hover or focus must be dismissible (without moving the pointer, e.g. via Escape), hoverable (the user can move the pointer onto the tooltip itself without it vanishing), and persistent (it stays until dismissed, focus moves, or it is no longer valid) — the three requirements of the WCAG content-on-hover-or-focus success criterion [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; corresponds to WCAG 1.4.13]. Every affordance must also be keyboard-focusable and expose its explanation to assistive tech (e.g. an accessible name/description), and on touch there must be a tap target, since hover does not exist. Accessibility is a hard constraint on the whole ladder, not an enhancement.

pros.claim: Meeting dismissible/hoverable/persistent and keyboard/touch access makes the help layer usable by everyone, not just mouse users
pros.example: tabbing to an info icon and reading its tooltip, then pressing Escape to dismiss it

cons.claim: Full accessibility adds implementation cost and constrains the visual/interaction design of every tooltip
cons.example: having to build focus handling and Escape dismissal for every hover card rather than a bare CSS title

failure_modes: shipping hover-only tooltips unreachable by keyboard or touch
tooltips that vanish before a user can move onto them or read them with assistive tech
acceptance_tests: the rung-2 spec requires dismissible/hoverable/persistent behavior, keyboard focus and assistive-tech exposure, and a touch tap target, tagged to the WCAG content-on-hover criterion as ESTIMATE — to source-verify
revisit_triggers: an accessibility audit finds hover-only content
a new WCAG version changes the requirements
touch users cannot reach an explanation

base.update_signal: an accessibility audit or a WCAG change tightens the requirements

nodes.definition: Catalog the failure patterns the help layer must avoid: (1) tooltip hell — burying so much in tooltips that the UI is unusable without hovering everything; (2) essential-info-in-a-tooltip — the only copy of something the user must act on lives behind a hover, so keyboard/touch/screen-reader users lose it; (3) hover-only on touch — a tooltip that never appears on a device with no pointer; (4) pointer hijacking / tooltip-on-everything — tooltips that block clicks, follow the cursor, or fire on non-informative elements, training users to ignore them. The avoidance rules: keep essentials on rung 1, make rung 2 accessible, reserve scent for surfaces that truly need it, and never let a tooltip be a required interaction path [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

included: pointer hijacking, each with an avoidance rule

pros.claim: An explicit anti-pattern list turns 'use tooltips well' into concrete rules a reviewer can check
pros.example: rejecting a design that puts the only 'this action is destructive' warning in a hover

cons.claim: Rules stated as absolutes can be over-applied, discouraging even the good, sparing tooltip use the ladder depends on
cons.example: banning all tooltips out of fear of tooltip hell and losing the useful rung-2 hints

failure_modes: putting the only copy of essential info in a tooltip
adding tooltips to everything until users learn to ignore them
acceptance_tests: the catalog names tooltip hell, essential-info-in-a-tooltip, hover-only-on-touch, and pointer hijacking, each paired with its avoidance rule
revisit_triggers: a review finds an anti-pattern shipped
tooltips are being ignored by users
a new tooltip misuse appears

base.update_signal: a shipped anti-pattern or ignored tooltips update the catalog

nodes.definition: Design the first-run experience for a brand-new user who has no cards, no reviews, and no data — the state where the app is emptiest and most confusing. The core move is empty-state onboarding: each empty surface explains itself and offers the first action (an empty Review queue says what a review is and links to add a card; an empty mastery view says it fills as you study), rather than a modal tour shown before the user has any context to attach it to [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. First-run help rides the same disclosure ladder — a short inline prompt with scent into a panel or the guide page — so onboarding is not a separate throwaway system but the ladder applied to the zero-data case.

excluded: the product-tour vs contextual-tip decision (own node)

pros.claim: Empty states that explain themselves teach the app at the moment of need without a blocking upfront tour
pros.example: an empty Review page reading 'No cards due yet — add or generate cards in Library to start' with a link

cons.claim: Empty-state copy only helps at the empty moment; once data exists the guidance is gone, so it cannot be the whole onboarding story
cons.example: a user who added cards on day one never seeing the empty-state hints again

failure_modes: showing a blocking modal tour before the user has context
leaving empty screens blank with no next action
acceptance_tests: the first-run design uses self-explaining empty states with first-action prompts and reuses the disclosure ladder rather than a separate upfront tour
revisit_triggers: new users still stall on the empty app
empty-state copy goes stale after a redesign
a data-seeded first run changes the empty case

base.update_signal: new users stalling or stale empty-state copy changes the first-run design

nodes.definition: Choose among onboarding patterns per situation: contextual just-in-time tips (a single hint at the moment a feature is first reachable), coach marks / spotlight callouts (a brief pointer to one control), and the guide page as the browsable reference — preferring pull (user asks) over push (app interrupts), and preferring one contextual tip over a linear product tour [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. The rule of thumb: teach a feature when the user arrives at it, not all features up front; let the ladder's scent carry the rest. A short optional tour can exist for orientation but must be skippable and never gate first use. Onboarding is thus a scheduling of the same ladder over the user's first sessions, not a distinct content system.

included: contextual tips vs coach marks vs guide-page reference

pros.claim: Just-in-time contextual tips teach each feature when it is relevant, which is remembered better than an upfront tour
pros.example: showing the desired-retention slider's one-line explanation the first time the user opens Settings, not on launch

cons.claim: Scattered contextual tips give no single overview, so a user wanting the big picture still needs the guide page
cons.example: a user who wants to understand the whole workflow before starting finding only piecemeal tips

failure_modes: defaulting to a linear forced tour
firing multiple tips at once and overwhelming the first session
acceptance_tests: the node picks contextual tips/coach marks/guide reference by situation, states pull-over-push and one-tip-over-tour heuristics, and keeps any tour optional and skippable
revisit_triggers: users want an overview the tips do not give
tips fire too densely
a new onboarding pattern is adopted

base.update_signal: a missing-overview complaint or tip density issue changes pattern selection

nodes.definition: Catalog the onboarding failures to avoid: (1) the tour dump — a multi-step forced modal tour of every feature before first use, retained by no one and skipped by most; (2) the onboarding cliff — help that appears exactly once and is unrecoverable afterward, so a user who dismissed it is stranded; (3) forced/blocking modals that gate the app behind acknowledgement; (4) re-nagging — showing the same tip every session because dismissal is not remembered. The mitigations: prefer contextual just-in-time help, make every explanation permanently re-reachable via scent and the guide page, never block first use, and persist dismissals [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; the onboarding-cliff risk is also flagged by the sysloops doctrine per SPECIALIST_LIST §C5].

pros.claim: Naming the onboarding cliff and tour dump lets a reviewer reject the two most common onboarding mistakes outright
pros.example: rejecting a launch-time modal tour in favor of recoverable contextual tips

cons.claim: Avoiding all upfront guidance can leave some users wanting a structured walkthrough that the anti-pattern rule discourages
cons.example: a user who would have liked a short optional tour finding none because tours were treated as forbidden

failure_modes: gating first use behind a forced tour
showing onboarding once with no way back
acceptance_tests: the catalog names tour dump, onboarding cliff, blocking modals, and re-nagging, each with its mitigation, and links the cliff risk to the sysloops doctrine reference
revisit_triggers: an onboarding anti-pattern ships
users ask for a structured walkthrough
dismissed tips reappear

base.update_signal: a shipped onboarding anti-pattern or a walkthrough request updates the catalog

nodes.definition: Architect the help system so the four rungs are one coherent system, not four disconnected copies. The guide page is the hub and canonical store; rungs 1-3 are spokes that quote or deep-link into it. Help is both embedded (in-context scent, tooltips, panels) and on-demand (the browsable guide page and search), and the two share content. The architecture assigns each concept a stable identifier so a tooltip, a panel, and a guide-page anchor all reference the same underlying explanation. This is what lets the app scale help across dozens of surfaces without the rungs contradicting each other, and it is greenfield because no help layer exists today [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9].

included: embedded plus on-demand help sharing content
excluded: the honesty of the content (own node)

pros.claim: A hub-and-spoke architecture keyed by concept id keeps every rung pointing at one explanation, so the system stays coherent as it grows
pros.example: the 'confidence' concept having one id that its tooltip, panel and guide anchor all resolve to

cons.claim: The shared-content architecture is more up-front structure than hard-coding strings per component and needs discipline to maintain
cons.example: having to register a concept id and source before adding a new tooltip

failure_modes: hard-coding independent copies per rung that then diverge
no stable concept id so deep links and shared content are impossible
acceptance_tests: the architecture makes the guide page the hub with rungs as spokes, shares content between embedded and on-demand help, and assigns each concept a stable identifier

nodes.definition: Place help where the confusion is: the scent affordance and its reveal attach directly to the element being explained, not in a distant help menu. A '?' next to 'confidence 80%' opens that concept's explanation; the info icon on the DayBox explains the DayBox. This proximity is what makes on-demand help feel like an answer rather than a search. Triggers are the explicit user actions that open a rung — hover/focus/tap for rung 2, click for rung 3, follow-link for rung 4 — and each is co-located with its subject [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. Contextual placement, driven by the information scent, is how the architecture reaches the user at the exact point of need.

failure_modes: burying explanations in a separate help section far from the confusing element

base.update_signal: ambiguous triggers or affordance noise changes placement

nodes.definition: Govern what the deep rungs SAY so the help layer is honest, not just present. When a rung explains an app number it must state that number's true nature. The load-bearing example: the Weakness 'confidence 80%' is rendered as Math.round(w.confidence*100)% of a per-rule HEURISTIC CONSTANT in the range 0.4-0.8 chosen by whichever E1-E4 diagnosis rule fired — it is NOT a computed posterior probability [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4a]. The explanation must say so plainly. This generalizes: the DayBox fill is a plan-progress ratio not a mastery measure; a mastery bar is an average of BKT estimates; 'New 24' is a per-day allowance not a deck size [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4b]. The exhaustive 'why the model produced this' derivation is deferred to the explainable-AI neighbor KB; this KB's duty is to refuse dishonest framing at every rung.

included: stating each surfaced number's true nature
the confidence-is-a-heuristic-constant rule as the anchor example

pros.claim: Requiring honest framing stops the help layer from laundering a heuristic constant into a scientific-looking probability
pros.example: a confidence tooltip reading 'fixed rule-of-thumb value, not a measured probability' instead of implying a computed 80%

cons.claim: Honest hedging can undercut user trust or confuse if worded clumsily, so plain-language care is required
cons.example: an explanation so full of caveats the user cannot tell what the number is for

failure_modes: presenting a fixed heuristic constant as a real probability
over-hedging until the explanation is useless
acceptance_tests: the rule requires each surfaced number's true nature to be stated, uses the confidence-is-a-heuristic-constant example cited to APP_RECON §4a, and defers the full why-derivation to the neighboring explainable-AI KB

the underlying app value changes meaning
the explainable-AI KB changes the scope seam

base.update_signal: a dishonestly framed number or a changed app value updates the honesty rule

nodes.definition: Remember what the user has already seen and dismissed so the help layer does not re-nag. A one-time onboarding tip, a coach mark, or a 'got it' dismissal must be persisted per user so it does not reappear every session, while the underlying explanation stays permanently re-reachable through scent and the guide page — the two together resolve the tension between not nagging and not stranding (the onboarding cliff) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. Contextual tooltips and the guide page are always available on demand; only the proactive, uninvited tips are suppressed after acknowledgement. A 'reset help / show tips again' control lets a user opt back in.

pros.example: a coach mark shown once, dismissed, and never repeated, with its content still in the guide page

cons.claim: Persisted state can hide help a user later wants, and single-user local state can be lost on reset

nodes.definition: Map the ladder onto the app's actual confusing surfaces so the design is concrete, not abstract. Worked examples [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4a-4c]: 'New 24' -> rung 1 relabel ('New cards today') is enough; the DayBox fill -> rung 1 caption plus a rung-2 tooltip ('fills 5% per unit of today's plan; check at 100%'); a mastery bar / 'FK6 Pathology' -> rung 2 tooltip plus a rung-3 panel explaining it averages BKT estimates over the INBDE blueprint axis; the Weakness 'confidence 80%' and the E1-E4 causes -> rungs 2-4, because the honest explanation (heuristic constant, not probability) and the four cause meanings need a panel and a guide-page anchor. This node is where the ladder, the honest-content rule and contextual triggers meet a real screen.

nodes.definition: Keep the rungs from drifting by single-sourcing: author each concept's explanation once in the guide-page source and derive the tooltip and panel copy from it, so a change made once propagates and the rungs cannot contradict each other or the UI. Governance mirrors the app's own metric discipline: every explanation has an owner concept id, and a term rename in the app triggers a review of its explanation. Because the guide layer is greenfield [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9], establishing single-sourcing at the start is far cheaper than reconciling divergent hard-coded strings later [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. This is the discipline that makes the help system maintainable rather than a growing pile of stale copies.

excluded: the honesty of the content (own node)

cons.claim: Single-sourcing adds authoring indirection that can feel heavier than typing a quick title= string

nodes.definition: Set the policy for HOW DEEP each concept's ladder goes, so the help layer stays proportionate: trivial, self-evident controls get rung 1 only; ambiguous labels and numbers get rungs 1-2; surfaces whose meaning is easily misread get a rung-3 panel; and algorithmic outputs that could mislead — the Weakness confidence, mastery aggregation, planner feasibility — earn all four rungs including a guide-page anchor and the honest-framing content. The escalation-depth budget prevents both under-serving a genuinely confusing number and over-building a four-rung ladder on a 'Save' button [ESTIMATE — design heuristic; to source-verify]. Depth is driven by risk of misreading, not by uniformity.

included: the four tiers of concept from trivial to algorithmic

pros.claim: A depth budget keyed to misreading risk spends help effort where confusion and honesty stakes are highest
pros.example: four rungs on 'confidence 80%' but a single relabel on a clear button

cons.claim: Judging misreading risk is subjective and can under-serve a surface one designer thinks is obvious
cons.example: leaving the DayBox at rung 1 because it looks self-evident when users still misread it as mastery

failure_modes: building four rungs uniformly regardless of need
under-serving a genuinely confusing algorithmic output
acceptance_tests: the policy sets ladder depth by risk of misreading across the four concept tiers and forbids both uniform over-building and under-serving algorithmic outputs
revisit_triggers: a surface is found under- or over-served

nodes.definition: Compose the go/no-go this KB builds toward. Go: build a four-rung disclosure ladder (inline caption -> accessible tooltip -> in-context 'more' panel -> canonical guide page) with visible, consistent information scent on every non-self-evident surface; single-source the content so rungs cannot drift; make first-run onboarding empty-state and contextual rather than an upfront tour; persist dismissed tips while keeping all explanations permanently re-reachable; set ladder depth by risk of misreading; and require every deep rung to state each number's true nature honestly — the Weakness 'confidence 80%' is a fixed heuristic constant, not a probability [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4a]. No-go: no forced/blocking product tour, no hover-only tooltips, no essential information hidden behind a reveal, and no dishonest framing of a heuristic as a measured quantity. A help surface earns its place only when it is discoverable, accessible, honest, and single-sourced.

the no-go on forced tours, hover-only tooltips, hidden essentials, and dishonest framing

priority_rationale: The problem frame and the progressive-disclosure principle come first because they decide that help is a layered on-demand system rather than upfront text; information scent and the four-rung ladder model come next as the spine every surface follows; the individual rungs (caption, accessible tooltip, expandable panel, guide page) and their anti-patterns then specify each step and its failure modes; first-run onboarding and the help-system architecture with contextual triggers and single-sourcing organize the content across surfaces; the honest-content rule governs what the deep rungs may say; and the surface mapping, escalation-depth policy, dismissal persistence and final verdict come last because they compose every upstream unit into a proportionate, accessible, honest, single-sourced help layer with an explicit no-go on forced tours, hover-only tooltips, hidden essentials, and dishonest framing.
